cards.front: A green plant builds its organic compounds from carbon dioxide, water and mineral nutrients. What can it not do, and what three things decide how it gets each mineral nutrient?
cards.back: It cannot make an element. How it gets each one depends on the element's form, how far that form moves, and who can take it up: the plant or a partner.
cards.quote: How it gets each mineral nutrient depends on three things: the form the element is in, how far that form moves

cards.front: An element is {{c1::essential}} if, without it, a plant cannot complete its life cycle from seed to seed.
cards.quote: An element is essential if, without it, a plant cannot complete its life cycle from seed to seed.
cards.section: What a plant must get from the soil

cards.front: Besides being needed to complete the life cycle, what two further conditions did Arnon and Stout set for an essential plant element?
cards.back: No other element can stand in for it, and it acts directly in the plant rather than by changing the soil or its microbes.
cards.quote: no other element can stand in for it, and it acts directly in the plant rather than by changing the soil or its microbes.
cards.section: What a plant must get from the soil

cards.front: The conventional list for vascular plants has {{c1::17}} essential elements.
cards.back: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from air and water; the other 14 are mineral nutrients.
cards.quote: The conventional list for vascular plants has 17 essential elements
cards.section: What a plant must get from the soil

cards.front: Name the six macronutrients of vascular plants (required in larger amounts).
cards.back: Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulfur.
cards.quote: Macronutrients (required in larger amounts): nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulfur.
cards.section: What a plant must get from the soil

cards.front: Name the eight micronutrients of vascular plants (required in trace amounts).
cards.back: Chlorine, boron, iron, manganese, copper, zinc, nickel and molybdenum.
cards.quote: Micronutrients (required in trace amounts): chlorine, boron, iron, manganese, copper, zinc, nickel and molybdenum.
cards.section: What a plant must get from the soil

cards.front: How does a beneficial plant element differ from an essential one? Give the role of sodium, silicon and cobalt.
cards.back: Beneficial elements improve growth in some species but are not universal requirements. Sodium helps some C4 or CAM plants, silicon strengthens grasses such as rice, and cobalt is used by nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume nodules.
cards.quote: Sodium helps some plants with C4 or CAM photosynthesis, silicon strengthens grasses such as rice, and cobalt is used by the nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume nodules.
cards.section: What a plant must get from the soil

cards.front: A nodulated pea in nitrogen-free solution grows poorly without cobalt, but a pea given mineral nitrogen grows from seed to seed without cobalt. By the Arnon and Stout criteria, is cobalt essential for the pea?
cards.back: No. The pea completes its life cycle without cobalt when given mineral nitrogen, and cobalt acts through the nodule bacteria, not directly in the plant. It counts as beneficial.
cards.why: Rests on two rules in the lesson: essentiality means the life cycle fails without the element, and the element must act directly in the plant.
cards.quote: cobalt is used by the nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume nodules
cards.section: What a plant must get from the soil

cards.front: How is a plant element tested for essentiality in water culture?
cards.back: Leave the one element out of a standard nutrient solution (such as Hoagland and Arnon's), see whether the plant fails, then put it back and see whether it recovers.
cards.quote: leaving one element out of it, then putting it back, is still the basic test.
cards.section: What a plant must get from the soil

cards.front: In testing whether barley needs nickel, why must the solution be made with purified salts and clean water?
cards.back: Nickel is needed in such small amounts that contamination from salts, water and the seed itself can supply it and hide a requirement.
cards.quote: Nickel is needed in such small amounts that contamination from salts, water and the seed itself can hide a requirement.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why must a test of whether barley needs nickel run through the whole life cycle and into the next generation?
cards.back: A seed carries nickel from its mother, so a first-generation plant may live on that store and look healthy even in nickel-free solution.
cards.quote: Run it for the whole life cycle and into the next generation, because a seed carries nickel from its mother
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Barley grown in nickel-depleted solution showed deficiency symptoms that adding nickel completely relieved, and its grain with less than 30 ng nickel per gram dry weight was not viable. What does this show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: Failure without nickel and rescue with it meet the criterion of a life cycle that cannot be completed without the element: nickel is essential for barley. It was one cereal in one preparation, so it gives no threshold for all plants or any fertiliser rate.
cards.quote: grain with less than 30 ng of nickel per gram of dry weight was not viable
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Rice grown without silicon has weaker stems. Is that enough to call silicon essential for rice? What would an essentiality test need to show?
cards.back: No. Weaker stems show only a benefit. A test would need plants in silicon-free solution that cannot complete the life cycle from seed to seed, rescue by add-back, no substitute element, and a direct action in the plant. The lesson lists silicon as beneficial.
cards.why: Rests on the Arnon and Stout criteria and the leave-out, add-back test.
cards.quote: Some lists add further elements, called beneficial: they improve growth in some species but are not universal requirements.
cards.section: What a plant must get from the soil

cards.front: Why do deficiencies of immobile elements tend to show first in new leaves and growing tips?
cards.back: Immobile elements stay largely where they were deposited, so new growth cannot draw on old leaves and depends mainly on what arrives from the roots.
cards.quote: For immobile elements, new leaves and growing tips depend mainly on what arrives from the roots
cards.section: Reading a sick leaf

cards.front: Without nitrogen the whole leaf yellows, {{c1::chlorosis}}, from lost chlorophyll.
cards.quote: Without nitrogen the whole leaf yellows, chlorosis, from lost chlorophyll
cards.section: Reading a sick leaf

cards.front: Japanese mint is grown in hydroponics with iron left out of the nutrient solution. Which leaves yellow first, and what does that suggest about iron's mobility in the phloem?
cards.back: The young leaves. In the mint study young leaves yellowed, consistent with iron being poorly mobile: it is not readily moved again from old leaves, so new growth depends on supply from the roots and shows the shortage first.
cards.quote: the whole blade of old leaves yellowed first without nitrogen, and young leaves yellowed without iron
cards.section: The Japanese mint deficiency study

cards.front: Why can't a young leaf or a fruit get more calcium from the roots?
cards.back: Calcium rides in xylem water and goes mostly where water leaves fastest by transpiration, the large mature leaves. It moves only poorly in the phloem, so young tissue gets little.
cards.quote: calcium rides in that water, so it goes mostly where water leaves fastest by transpiration
cards.section: Reading a sick leaf

cards.front: Developing fruit are enclosed so the air around them stays very humid, while the leaves keep transpiring hard. Predict the effect on the calcium the fruit receive, and explain.
cards.back: Less calcium reaches the fruit. Calcium follows xylem water to where water leaves fastest, now even more to the leaves, and poor phloem mobility of calcium cannot make up the difference.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's rule that calcium travels with transpiration water and moves poorly in the phloem.
cards.quote: Young leaves and fruit lose much less water, so they receive less, and calcium moves only poorly in the phloem
cards.section: Reading a sick leaf

cards.front: A leaf symptom suggests a nutrient deficiency. Why is the symptom only a hypothesis, and how is it tested and then confirmed?
cards.back: Different deficiencies look alike, and drought, disease or cold can mimic them. Tissue analysis (measuring the leaf's elements) tests it; add-back (supplying the element and watching new growth recover) confirms it.
cards.quote: Tissue analysis, measuring the elements in the leaf, tests it; add-back, supplying the suspected element and watching new growth recover, confirms it.
cards.section: Reading a sick leaf

cards.front: Old tomato leaves yellow after a cold spell. Tissue analysis shows normal leaf nitrogen, and adding nitrogen gives no recovery in new growth. What do you conclude?
cards.back: Nitrogen deficiency is not supported. Both tests failed to back the hypothesis; cold can mimic a deficiency, so look for another cause.
cards.quote: Different deficiencies can look alike, and drought, disease or cold can mimic them, so a symptom is a hypothesis.
cards.section: Reading a sick leaf

cards.front: As a general pattern, how do many plants short of magnesium look?
cards.back: Older leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay green.
cards.quote: many plants short of magnesium yellow between the veins of older leaves while the veins stay green
cards.section: The Japanese mint deficiency study

cards.front: A 10 mm root segment, 0.5 mm in diameter, carries 1,000 root hairs, each 0.5 mm long and 0.010 mm wide. Treating each as a cylinder and ignoring the ends (side area = pi x d x L), by how much do the hairs raise the segment's surface?
cards.back: Root: pi x 0.5 x 10 = 15.7 mm2. One hair: pi x 0.010 x 0.5 = 0.0157 mm2; 1,000 hairs = 15.7 mm2. Total 31.4 mm2: the hairs double the surface. Illustrative numbers.
cards.quote: The hairs double the surface, to 31.4 mm2.
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: The same root segment (15.7 mm2, plus 15.7 mm2 of hairs) also carries 1 m (1,000 mm) of mycorrhizal hyphae, each 0.004 mm wide. What surface do the hyphae add, and what is the new total?
cards.back: Hyphae: pi x 0.004 mm x 1,000 mm = 12.6 mm2. Total: 15.7 + 15.7 + 12.6 = 44.0 mm2. Illustrative numbers.
cards.quote: The total is now 15.7 + 15.7 + 12.6 = 44.0 mm2.
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: For a cylinder with ends ignored, surface per volume = {{c1::4 / d}}.
cards.back: d is the diameter: the thinner the cylinder, the more surface per unit of material.
cards.quote: surface per volume of a cylinder = 4 / d
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: Using surface per volume = 4 / d, compare a root 0.5 mm wide, a root hair 0.010 mm wide and a hypha 0.004 mm wide (mm2 of surface per mm3 of material).
cards.back: Root: 4 / 0.5 = 8. Hair: 4 / 0.010 = 400. Hypha: 4 / 0.004 = 1,000. The hypha gives 125 times the root's surface per unit of material.
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: A 10 mm root segment 0.5 mm wide has 15.7 mm2 of surface; 1,000 mm of hyphae 0.004 mm wide add 12.6 mm2. Compare the hyphae's volume with the root's (volume = pi x r2 x L).
cards.back: Hyphae: pi x (0.002 mm)2 x 1,000 mm = 0.013 mm3. Root: pi x (0.25 mm)2 x 10 mm = 2.0 mm3. The hyphae add about 80% of the root's surface for under 1% (about 0.6%) of its volume.
cards.quote: the hyphae occupy pi x (0.002 mm)2 x 1,000 mm = 0.013 mm3, against 2.0 mm3 for the root segment.
cards.section: Surface per volume: the volume check

cards.front: Phosphate around a root becomes depleted. Combining the trade with fungi and the surface-per-volume rule, why is a mycorrhiza an economical way for a plant to reach more phosphate?
cards.back: The fungus extends reach beyond the depletion zone, and its thin hyphae give far more surface per unit of material than root (1,000 vs 8 mm2 per mm3). The plant pays carbon, though the root still takes up phosphate itself.
cards.why: Rests on surface per volume = 4 / d and the lesson's description of the carbon-for-reach trade.
cards.quote: the plant pays carbon, and the fungus extends its reach beyond the depletion zone, though the root still takes up phosphate itself
cards.section: Borrowing nitrogen and phosphorus: nodules and mycorrhizae

cards.front: Root hairs help with phosphate uptake. What evidence shows they do not help water uptake reliably everywhere?
cards.back: In barley, root hairs aided water extraction by rapidly transpiring plants in drying soil, but a hairless maize mutant took up water no differently in sand or loam.
cards.quote: a hairless maize mutant took up water no differently in sand or loam
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: The {{c1::apoplast}} is the cell walls and the spaces between them, outside the living membranes.
cards.back: Water and ions seep along it through the outer root without entering a cell.
cards.quote: The apoplast is the cell walls and the spaces between them, outside the living membranes
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: What is the symplast in a root, and how does an ion enter it?
cards.back: The living cytoplasm, joined cell to cell by plasmodesmata. An ion enters by crossing a plasma membrane once, through a transporter or channel, then passes cell to cell without crossing another.
cards.quote: The symplast is the living cytoplasm, joined from cell to cell by plasmodesmata, narrow channels through the walls.
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: What is the Casparian strip, and where does it run?
cards.back: A band in the walls between endodermal cells (the single ring around the central cylinder) that seals the wall route.
cards.quote: In the walls between endodermal cells runs the Casparian strip, a band that seals the wall route.
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: Why is the endodermis called the root's checkpoint?
cards.back: Where the Casparian strip is complete, an ion in the walls must cross a plasma membrane into a living cell. So whatever reaches the xylem has passed through a living cell whose transporters and channels could have kept it out.
cards.quote: whatever reaches the xylem has passed through a living cell, whose transporters and channels could have kept it out
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: A mutant root has gaps in its Casparian strip. Predict what happens to an ion that the endodermal cells' transporters would normally keep out.
cards.back: It can leak through the walls into the central cylinder and reach the xylem without crossing a membrane. The checkpoint holds only where the strip is complete.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the strip seals the wall route, forcing passage through a living cell.
cards.quote: The root's checkpoint holds where the Casparian strip is complete.

cards.front: What is the Casparian strip made of in young Arabidopsis roots?
cards.back: Lignin, not suberin as older textbooks say; suberin is laid down later.
cards.quote: In young Arabidopsis roots the strip is lignin, not suberin as older textbooks say
cards.section: What the Casparian strip is made of, and a second barrier

cards.front: Why does taking up an anion such as nitrate or phosphate into a root cell often cost energy?
cards.back: The cell interior is negative, so the voltage pushes an anion back, and often its concentration gradient does too.
cards.quote: The inside of a root cell is negative, so an anion, a negative ion such as nitrate or phosphate, is pushed back by the voltage
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: How do root cells power nitrate uptake?
cards.back: An ATP-driven H+-ATPase pumps protons out. A transporter then often lets a proton flow back in down its gradient, carrying nitrate (or another ion) with it: cotransport.
cards.quote: Transporters then let a proton flow back in, down its gradient, carrying nitrate or another ion with it
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: A drug blocks the plasma-membrane H+-ATPase of root cells. Predict the effect on nitrate uptake, and explain.
cards.back: Nitrate uptake falls. Without proton pumping the proton gradient runs down, so there is little inward proton flow to drive nitrate cotransport against the negative interior.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's rule that the pump's proton gradient powers proton-nitrate cotransport.
cards.quote: A proton pump, an ATP-driven H+-ATPase in the plasma membrane, moves protons out of root cells.
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: A nitrate ion moves through the cortex walls and reaches the endodermis. What must happen for it to reach the xylem, and why does that step often need energy?
cards.back: The Casparian strip seals the walls, so nitrate must cross a plasma membrane into a living cell. The interior is negative, pushing the anion back, so entry often uses proton cotransport powered by the ATP-driven H+-ATPase.
cards.why: Combines the checkpoint rule with the energetics of anion uptake.
cards.quote: Where the strip is complete, an ion travelling in the walls must cross a plasma membrane into a living cell
cards.section: Into the root: hairs, two routes and a checkpoint

cards.front: What are the main nitrogen forms a root takes up, and why can't a plant use the nitrogen gas around it?
cards.back: Nitrate and ammonium. No plant enzyme can use nitrogen gas.
cards.quote: Nitrate and ammonium are the main nitrogen forms a root takes up.
cards.section: Borrowing nitrogen and phosphorus: nodules and mycorrhizae

cards.front: Nitrogenase is damaged by oxygen, yet the bacteroids that make it respire. How does the nodule resolve this?
cards.back: The plant protein leghemoglobin binds oxygen and buffers it at a low, steady level. It does not exclude oxygen.
cards.quote: A plant protein, leghemoglobin, binds oxygen and buffers it at a low, steady level; it does not exclude oxygen.
cards.section: Borrowing nitrogen and phosphorus: nodules and mycorrhizae

cards.front: Leghemoglobin genes are silenced in Lotus japonicus. Predict nodule oxygen, nitrogen fixation, and growth with and without mineral nitrogen. What does the result show?
cards.back: Free oxygen rises, fixation stops, and plants grow normally only with mineral nitrogen. Leghemoglobin is needed for fixation, not for growth itself.
cards.quote: Free oxygen in the nodules rose, fixation stopped, and the plants grew normally only when given mineral nitrogen
cards.section: Silencing leghemoglobin

cards.front: Invented practice numbers: pea seeds holding 10 mg nitrogen each grow in nitrogen-free sand. With live soil extract, plants form nodules and contain 95 mg nitrogen; with heat-treated extract, no nodules and 9 mg. How much nitrogen did each nodulated plant gain from the air, and what does the heat-treated group show?
cards.back: 95 - 10 = 85 mg from the air (the only other source is the seed). The heat-treated group gained no nitrogen and had no nodules, so something in the live extract that heat destroys is needed for fixation.
cards.quote: The 1888 pots did not identify the living agent behind the nodules, the root swellings
cards.section: Borrowing nitrogen and phosphorus: nodules and mycorrhizae

cards.front: Describe arbuscular mycorrhizae: how widespread they are, and where nutrients are exchanged.
cards.back: They form in most land plants. Hyphae push through cortex cell walls and branch into arbuscules, tree-like structures wrapped in the plant's folded cell membrane, where nutrients are exchanged.
cards.quote: Hyphae push through the walls of cortex cells and branch into arbuscules, tree-like structures wrapped in the plant's folded cell membrane, where nutrients are exchanged.
cards.section: Borrowing nitrogen and phosphorus: nodules and mycorrhizae

cards.front: In arbuscular mycorrhizae, what does the fungus give the plant, and what does the plant pay?
cards.back: The fungus delivers minerals from soil, especially phosphate. The plant pays in sugars, and (shown in Lotus japonicus) in lipids as well.
cards.quote: The fungus delivers minerals taken from soil, especially phosphate.
cards.section: Borrowing nitrogen and phosphorus: nodules and mycorrhizae

cards.front: How do ectomycorrhizae differ from arbuscular mycorrhizae in structure and in what they supply?
cards.back: They form on trees such as pines and oaks and help supply nitrogen. The fungus sheathes the root tip and grows a network between root cells without entering them.
cards.quote: The fungus wraps the root tip in a sheath and grows a network between root cells without entering them
cards.section: Borrowing nitrogen and phosphorus: nodules and mycorrhizae

cards.front: How could you show that a plant pays its arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus in carbon, and what did such work find in Lotus japonicus?
cards.back: Label carbon in the plant (isotope labelling) and look for it in the fungus; compare plant mutants. Keymer and colleagues found the plant pays in sugars and in lipids as well.
cards.quote: Keymer and colleagues (2017) showed with isotope labelling and plant mutants that it pays in lipids as well.
cards.section: Borrowing nitrogen and phosphorus: nodules and mycorrhizae

cards.front: How does the purple pitcher plant, Sarracenia purpurea, get extra nitrogen in a nitrogen-poor bog?
cards.back: It still photosynthesizes. Insects drown in rainwater in its pitchers, where bacteria, protists and larvae break them down, releasing mineral nitrogen, while also competing with the plant for it.
cards.quote: Insects drown in rainwater held in the pitchers, where bacteria, protists and larvae break them down, releasing mineral nitrogen
cards.section: Plants that eat animals and plants that tap plants

cards.front: Microbes in a pitcher break prey down to mineral nitrogen. Why does finding plant uptake of a labelled amino acid only suggest, not prove, direct amino-acid uptake, and what result would strengthen the case?
cards.back: The data were consistent with direct uptake, clearest for phenylalanine. But microbes could break the label down to mineral nitrogen first, so label in the plant might arrive in mineral form. Finding the intact labelled amino acid in plant tissue would plausibly favour direct uptake (an inference).
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's points that pitcher microbes release mineral nitrogen and that the data were only consistent with direct uptake.
cards.quote: added labelled amino acids to pitchers in Ontario and Massachusetts and found data consistent with direct amino-acid uptake by the plant
cards.section: Plants that eat animals and plants that tap plants

cards.front: How does dodder (Cuscuta), a twining stem parasite, get resources from its host?
cards.back: It forms haustoria that grow into the host stem and connect to its xylem and phloem, drawing water, nutrients and sugars.
cards.quote: it forms haustoria, organs that grow into the host stem and connect to its xylem and phloem
cards.section: Plants that eat animals and plants that tap plants

cards.front: A pea, a pine, a purple pitcher plant and dodder each borrow from another organism. For each, name the partner and which factor (form, distance, or who can take it up) the partnership solves.
cards.back: Pea: rhizobia turn unusable nitrogen gas into ammonia (form). Pine: ectomycorrhizal fungi help supply nitrogen. Pitcher plant: insects and the pitcher food web supply nitrogen scarce in the bog. Dodder: taps a host's xylem and phloem for water, nutrients and sugars.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's one idea: form, how far it moves, and who can take it up.
cards.quote: A pea borrows from bacteria, a pine from fungi, a pitcher plant from insects and a food web, and dodder from another plant.
cards.section: Plants that eat animals and plants that tap plants
